reason: Researched (WebSearch, WebFetch of Delta's Oct-9 8-K and TradingEconomics Brent page, Yahoo daily closes). The book is a deliberate two-sided bet on the Hormuz outcome: 35% low-beta refiners (MPC/PSX/VLO, +3 to +5% on the leg) gain if the product squeeze persists, 27% airlines (JETS/UAL, -1.6%/-2.3%) gain if a deal deflates fuel, and 38% cash is the clean deal hedge. This week's news hit both sides without breaking either. Brent is ~$104 with Iran 'reviewing' a US proposal to reopen Hormuz within 7 days, 11 tankers were attacked in the week to Oct 4, and Trump says no new strikes before the midterms, so the outcome is still binary and the hedge structure is right. On refiners, the US issued a temporary license for ~22.5M bbl of Russian diesel and China resumes product exports, and heating oil fell ~3% on Oct 9 while MPC/VLO gave back ~2%. But Hormuz carries mostly crude, not products, Gulf refineries remain offline, and late-October Q3 prints will show record-crack earnings, so I keep the low-beta refiners rather than chase or dump. I am honest that the airline leg's original premise of management-quantified fuel relief was dented: Delta missed Q3 ($1.72 vs ~$2.02), cut FY EPS to $5.10-5.60 from $6.50-7.50, and guided Q4 fuel to ~$4.25/gal. Yet DAL closed flat on the day (82.14 to 82.17), which says the fuel pain is priced, and the airlines now act as the book's main lever on a Hormuz deal. UAL reports this week and its 18% stop caps that event risk. Every leg is far from its stop and take-profit, the book is +10.76% with a -5.22% max drawdown, and a full or partial rebalance would cost basis points without changing the exposure I want. So I hold.
